## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-09.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Why is knowledge of IT architecture useful?

Writing software is not enough; it must also be operated so that it is
available
able to operate under load
secure
quickly recoverable
cost-effective

This requires specialized IT operations (Ops) knowledge.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-10.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
What does Ops do?

Operates servers
Builds and configures networks and infrastructure
Monitors systems
Ensures security
Handles incidents
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-11.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Earlier trends

Development (Dev) and Operations (Ops) were completely separated
Developers (Dev) wrote the software
Then handed it over to Operations
In case of a software bug, the code went back to the developers
Slow, cumbersome communication
Many conflicts
No one had an overview of both areas
:::

integrated

DevOps

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-15.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Historical overview

From the beginnings … abacus, slide rule …
Mechanical computers (Schickard, Pascal, Babbage)
Electromechanical computers (Zuse)
Electronic computers  computer generations
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-16.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Abacus (3rd millennium BC), slide rule (~1620)

Primarily used for addition and subtraction
The rods represent place values, while the beads represent digit values

Abacus Simulator (uni-marburg.de)

Slide Rule Simulator Emulator Replica Collection
Scales that slide relative to each other
In addition to basic arithmetic, it can be used to calculate roots, logarithms, and trigonometric functions
Accuracy of 3–4 decimal digits
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-17.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Schickard’s calculating machine (1623)

Capable of performing the four basic arithmetic operations
Mechanical design: 
   6 pairs of gears     	(with10 and 1 tooth)
Handled carry operations automatically
The prototype under construction was destroyed in a fire
Two replicas were built much later

Multiplication with the Schickard Calculator from 1623 and
with Napier's Bones - YouTube
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-18.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Pascal’s adding machine (1643)

Built using clock components
Addition and subtraction only
Also handled carry operations
Pascal built 7 machines

Pascaline – interactive simulations –
eduMedia (edumedia-sciences.com)


How the Pascaline Works - YouTube
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-19.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Babbage’s Difference Engine (~1820)

Mechanical computer
15 tonnes
25,000 components
Decimal number system
Its construction was mainly hindered by technical limitations
A working machine based on Babbage’s plans was not completed until 1991
31-digit representation
Mathematical (polynomial) tables

Babbage's Difference Engine Simulation (drexel.edu)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-20.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Babbage’s Analytical Engine

Programmable using punched cards
Designed to store programs (addressable memory)
Printer
A precursor of modern computers
The machine itself was never fully built, but programs were designed for it (Ada Lovelace)
Web Analytical Engine Emulator (fourmilab.ch)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-21.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Zuse’s computers (Z1, Z2, Z3 …, from ~1941)

Electromechanical computers (relays)
More reliable than vacuum-tube computers
Binary number system
Program–controlled operation (Z3)
Stored-program concept? (not published)
Zuse Z3 (historicsimulations.com)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-22.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Computer generations

Generations are the major stages in computer evolution.

We distinguish 5 generations
6th generation?
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-23.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
First-generation computers (~1945–55)

Vacuum-tube computers
Large size and weight
Magnetic drum memory
Unreliable operation
Machine code
Expensive
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-24.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
ENIAC (1946)

Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer
Massive hardware
18,000 vacuum tubes
30 tonnes
2.5 m high, 30 m long
Operation time on the order of milliseconds
Decimal number system
Military purposes (ballistic calculations)
eniacrun.png (1900×1070) (drexel.edu)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-25.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
EDVAC (1949)

Electronic Discrete -Variable Automatic Computer
John von Neumann also participated in its development
General-purpose computer
Program stored in memory
Binary arithmetic
Input via a typewriter-like device
Output via a printer

EDVAC - YouTube
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-26.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Second-generation computers (~1955–65)

Transistors
(much smaller and more reliable than vacuum tubes)
Produced in larger quantities (e.g. about 17,000 IBM 1400-series systems)
Modular design
Emergence of the first high-level programming languages (COBOL, Fortran)
~10⁵–10⁶ operations/s
Batch processing – less idle time
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-27.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Third-generation computers (~1965–72)

Integrated circuits (ICs)
Smaller size and greater reliability – minicomputers also appeared
Operating systems
Keyboards and monitors became common
Sales in the hundreds of thousands
Semiconductor memory
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-28.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Fourth-generation computers (~1972–)

Microprocessor
High level of integration (LSI, VLSI, ULSI)
100 million operations/s
Personal computers
Graphical user interface
Mouse
Small size
Low cost
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-29.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Fifth-generation computers (1986–)

Artificial intelligence
Speech recognition
Natural-language input
Learning capability
Parallel processing
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-30.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
The development of semiconductors drives progress

“The number of transistors on chips roughly doubles every two years” (Gordon Moore, 1965)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-31.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Computer

Computer  Calculator

A computer is a device capable of storing data and sequences of operations (programs) defined by humans and executing them automatically

In a broader sense, the following devices can also be considered computers:
Game consoles (Xbox, PlayStation)
Embedded systems (mobile phones, smart devices, engine control electronics, GPS, etc.)
some IoT* devices

*IoT = Internet of Things
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-32.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Embedded systems

Special-purpose computers designed to perform a specific task

They do not look like computers from the outside
They are usually small, but can also be large (e.g. traffic-light controllers)
Their architecture usually includes:
Central processing unit
Sensors
Output/communication interface
Actuators (convert signals, e.g. into motion)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-33.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
IoT – Internet of Things

Devices equipped with computing capability and network connectivity

This also includes “smart” embedded systems. 

Characteristics:
Utility
Intelligence
Dynamic nature
Heterogeneity
Security?
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-34.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Components of a computer

Three main functional components: processor, memory and I/O unit
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-35.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
The bus system

A set of communication lines connecting the functional components of a computer.
Types:
Control bus
Address bus
Data bus
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-36.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Von Neumann principles

Stored-program concept
(data and instructions are stored in the same memory in the same way)
Sequential instruction execution
A fully electronic machine operating with the binary number system
Functional units: separate input/output unit, control and processing unit, and memory
General-purpose applicability
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-37.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
The von Neumann architecture problem

The main problem of the architecture is that the processor often has to wait for memory operations, so most of its processing time is unused
(“von Neumann bottleneck”)

Other architectures also exist, e.g.:
Harvard architecture
Parallel architectures
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-38.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Harvard architecture

Separate data and instruction memory
Greater security
Better performance
More complex design
Applications:
Microcontrollers
CPUs
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-39.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Parallel architecture

Processing multiple data items and/or instructions simultaneously
Higher performance
Several models
More difficult to program
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-40.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Parallel architecture – example

UMA – Uniform Memory Access
The processors share memory equally
Either all processors have equal access to peripherals (symmetric multiprocessing) or only certain processors do (asymmetric multiprocessing)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-41.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Aside: quantum computers

They operate based on
quantum mechanics
Quantum bits (qubits) instead of bits
Two key properties
Superposition
Entanglement
Compared with conventional computers,
they can be many orders of magnitude faster
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-42.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Quantum computers

Challenges:
Sensitive even to very small disturbances
As the number of qubits increases,
error detection and correction become increasingly difficult
They require new algorithms and
software

It may still take 10–30 years before
they become widespread

Image source
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-43.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
The processor (CPU – Central Processing Unit)

The central processing unit of the computer interprets and executes
instructions
Components:
Control Unit
Arithmetic Logic Unit
Registers
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-44.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
The Control Unit (CU)

The part of the processor that

Controls data flow between the ALU and the registers
Interprets
instructions
Converts instructions into
control signals
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-45.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
The machine instruction cycle

Fetch: read the address of the next instruction
from the PC
register
Decode: decode the instruction stored in the IR
Execute: the CPU passes the required information to the ALU, which executes the instruction

Image source: https://computersciencewiki.org/index.php/The_machine_ instruction_cycle
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-46.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)

Performs arithmetic and logical
operations.

Basic operations:
Boolean operations
Binary addition
Complement operation
Bit shifting
right/left

Image source
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-47.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Registers

Small, very fast storage locations
Typically 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits wide
Usually implemented as static storage
They can store

Data: AX, BX, CX, DX
Memory addresses: SI, DI, SP, BP, CS, DS, SS, ES, IR
Status and control

information: PC, IR, flags

Image source
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-48.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
CISC and RISC processors

CISC
Complex instruction set   
Compound instructions
One instruction – multiple clock cycles   
One register set
Longer execution time

RISC
Reduced instruction set  
Simple instructions
One instruction – one clock cycle   
Multiple register sets
Shorter execution time

CISC = Complex Instruction Set Computers
RISC = Reduced Instruction Set Computers
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-49.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Main memory

Stores programs currently being executed and the data they require
Random access
(RAM – Random Access Memory)
The processor can access and address it directly
Its contents are lost when power is turned off
Usually dynamic RAM (DRAM) – requires refreshing
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-50.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Memory addressing

Main addressing modes
(addresses are hexadecimal)
Direct memory addressing
Segment:offset addressing
(segment register + offset)
Indirect addressing (the address is stored in a register)
Base-relative addressing (base register + offset)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-51.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Memory addressing

Segment-offset addressing

Direct memory addressing
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-52.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Memory addressing

Base-relative addressing

Indirect memory addressing
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-53.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Memory hierarchy

Cache memory bridges the speed gap between components operating at different speeds
It has multiple levels; e.g. Level 1 cache between the CPU and main memory
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-54.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
The I/O unit (peripherals)

Input devices
(e.g. mouse, keyboard)
Output devices
(e.g. printer, monitor)
I/O devices (e.g. hard disk drive)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-55.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Ports

A PORT is a computer
interface used to communicate with peripheral devices.
It provides a standardized
connection between the CPU and peripherals via the system bus (external bus).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-56.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Serial and parallel data transmission

When data is transferred between the peripheral interface and the peripheral one bit at a time, sequentially, this is called serial data transmission.
(e.g. mouse, modem)
When groups of bits are transferred simultaneously between the peripheral interface and the peripheral, this is called parallel data transmission (e.g. printer).
USB – high-speed serial transmission
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-01/slide-57.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Interrupts

The currently executing activity is suspended
The data required to resume execution must be saved
The interrupt service routine must be started

The interrupt

must be completed,

and the original state must be restored
Causes of interrupts: I/O devices, errors, keystrokes, etc.
:::
